# The Rising Sun Casts Long Shadows: Sumo's Reckoning

For centuries, sumo has stood as something more than sport in Japan—a living Shinto ritual, a repository of national character, its wrestlers regarded as vessels of tradition rather than mere athletes. But in recent years, that carefully maintained image has cracked open, revealing troubles that mirror the struggles of any modern professional sport: violence, drugs, corruption. And at the center of the storm has stood one man whose talent was undeniable and whose behavior became a lightning rod for a sport confronting its own contradictions—Asashoryu.

## The Mongolian Wolf

Asashoryu Akinori, born Dolgorsuren Dagvadorj in Ulaanbaatar, arrived in Japan's sumo world as an outsider in every sense. He rose through the ranks with a ferocity that earned him the nickname "the Mongolian Wolf," becoming yokozuna—sumo's highest rank—in 2003. He was, by many measures, one of the most dominant wrestlers of his generation.

But dominance came paired with controversy. Asashoryu was repeatedly cited for conduct unbecoming a yokozuna—a rank that demands *hinkaku*, or dignity, as much as it demands strength. He was suspended in 2007 after being caught playing in a charity soccer match while supposedly too injured to compete in a tour. Photographs of him grinning and roughhousing overseas, contrasted with his claimed injuries, ignited a firestorm in the Japanese press. Critics called him arrogant, foreign, disrespectful of tradition. Supporters countered that he was being held to a standard no wrestler—Japanese or otherwise—could sustain, and that xenophobia colored much of the criticism.

Asashoryu's career ultimately ended in 2010 following an altercation outside a Tokyo nightclub in which he allegedly assaulted a man, breaking his nose. Rather than face formal sanction, he announced his retirement. It was an ignominious exit for a wrestler many considered among the greatest of all time—but it was also, in retrospect, an early tremor before the earthquake.

## The Scandals Multiply

In the years since, sumo's institutional crisis has only deepened, suggesting Asashoryu's troubles were symptomatic of something larger festering within the sport's closed, hierarchical culture.

**Match-fixing** allegations surfaced most explosively in 2011, when police investigating illegal baseball gambling among wrestlers stumbled onto text messages revealing arranged bout outcomes—wrestlers discussing payments to throw matches, coded language about "working together." The Japan Sumo Association was forced to cancel an entire tournament, the first cancellation in the sport's modern history for reasons other than war. More than a dozen wrestlers were expelled. The scandal struck at sumo's very claim to legitimacy: if outcomes could be bought, what remained of the ritual combat between purely trained bodies?

**Drug bans** followed, further corroding the image of sumo as a uniquely disciplined pursuit. Wrestlers were found using marijuana—a stunning revelation in a sport whose practitioners are meant to embody purity in the Shinto sense, performing purification rituals before every bout. Several were dismissed, their stables (training houses) publicly shamed, and questions raised about the insular *heya* system that governs young wrestlers' lives with near-total control and minimal outside oversight.

**The death of a trainee** proved the most devastating revelation of all. In 2007, a seventeen-year-old wrestler named Takashi Saito, competing under the name Tokitaizan, died after being beaten by his stablemaster and senior wrestlers as punishment for attempting to run away from training. The stablemaster, Tokitsukaze, was eventually convicted, along with three wrestlers, of assault resulting in death. The case exposed the brutal disciplinary culture within stables—the beatings passed off as tradition, the code of silence that let it continue, the vulnerability of teenage boys handed over to institutions with total authority over their bodies and futures.

## A Sport at the Crossroads

Taken together, these scandals paint a picture of an institution straining under the weight of its own mythology. Sumo has always demanded that its wrestlers be more than athletes—they are meant to be moral exemplars, living connections to a Shinto past, disciplined ascetics performing a national ideal. That demand for *hinkaku*, for dignity, is precisely what was invoked against Asashoryu again and again.

Yet the deeper scandals—fixed matches, drug use, a teenager beaten to death—suggest that the sport's failures were never really about individual wrestlers falling short of an impossible standard. They were about a closed system that operated with minimal transparency, where stablemasters held near-total power over young recruits, where gambling and corruption could flourish specifically because outside scrutiny was treated as an insult to tradition.

Asashoryu, for all his genuine transgressions, became a convenient face for anxieties that ran much deeper—about foreign wrestlers dominating a "Japanese" sport, about changing values, about a public increasingly uncomfortable with institutions that claimed sacred status while asking for exemption from ordinary accountability. He was sumo's most visible controversy, but not its most serious one.

The Japan Sumo Association has since instituted reforms: an outside conduct committee, stricter oversight of stables, hotlines for wrestlers to report abuse. Whether these changes penetrate a culture built on absolute hierarchy and unquestioning obedience to seniors remains sumo's central, unresolved question—one that will determine whether the sport can survive as something more than a beautiful, dangerous relic.
